image_description: A male mallard duck (drake) standing on a grassy bank near water. The duck features the characteristic iridescent green head, white neck ring, chestnut breast, and grey/brown body plumage. It has a yellow bill with a black tip, dark eyes, and orange webbed feet visible on the grass. The background consists of blurred dry branches and water.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Most distinctive feature is the broad, flat bill adapted for filter-feeding; bill is dark grey to yellow-green.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The bill is clearly visible, broad, and flat. The color is predominantly yellow-orange with a darker tip, which fits the 'yellow-green' to 'dark grey' spectrum described for drakes (specifically mallards often have yellow bills).
The eye is visible and appears dark/black, consistent with the taxonomy.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Body is stocky and compact, streamlined and buoyant with dense waterproof plumage.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The body shape is robust and streamlined. The plumage appears dense and smooth, indicative of waterproof feathers.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Breeding plumage is typically more colorful than female: common patterns include iridescent green head with white neck ring and grey body (mallard), or chestnut head with grey body.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The image perfectly matches the Mallard drake description: iridescent green head, distinct white neck ring, chestnut breast, and grey/flank body.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Legs are short and set far back on the body with webbed feet (three forward toes connected by webbing).
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The legs are orange and positioned towards the rear of the body. The feet are visible on the grass, showing the characteristic webbed structure of an aquatic bird.
The folded wing is visible along the side of the body, appearing broad and structurally sound.

checkpoint_verdicts.checkpoint: Tail is short with curled central tail feathers (drake feathers) in many species.
checkpoint_verdicts.reasoning: The tail is short. While the specific 'curl' of the central feathers is subtle due to the angle, the general tail structure is present and correct for a drake.
